skill.name: home-assistant-manager
skill.description: Guides AI assistants through Home Assistant configuration, deployment, validation, automation testing, log review, and Lovelace dashboard workflows using SSH, hass-cli, git, and scp.
skill.summary: Manage Home Assistant configuration, automations, and dashboards with deployment and verification workflows.
skill.author: komal-SkyNET

security_audit.summary: The skill is not malicious, but it intentionally guides privileged Home Assistant operations through SSH, hass-cli, git, and scp. Confirmed risks center on remote command execution, writing Home Assistant .storage files, persistent token setup, and commands that can affect real devices; many scanner hits were Markdown, template, or screenshot false positives. No prompt injection attempt was found in the reviewed files.

remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user confirmation before SSH, scp, hass-cli service calls, automation triggers, git pull on /config, reloads, or restarts. Show the exact target host and expected side effects first.

remediation.issue: Long-lived tokens in shell startup files
remediation.suggestion: Recommend a secret manager, session-scoped environment variables, or restricted credentials where possible. Warn users not to commit, log, screenshot, or share HASS_TOKEN values.

remediation.issue: Direct writes to Home Assistant .storage files
remediation.suggestion: Back up .storage files before copying, validate dashboard JSON first, and require review before modifying lovelace_dashboards or restarting Home Assistant.
Document that Context7 uses an external network service and a user-provided API key. Keep that key out of shared configuration and logs.

semantic_findings.title: Long-Lived Home Assistant Token in Shell Profile
semantic_findings.description: The README tells users to add HASS_SERVER and HASS_TOKEN values to shell startup files. A Home Assistant token stored there can be exposed to shells, subprocesses, backups, or accidental sharing.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The setup instructions explicitly name ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc and then export HASS_TOKEN on the following line. This is a real secret persistence risk, although it is normal setup guidance rather than malicious behavior.

semantic_findings.title: Automation Trigger Commands Can Affect Physical Devices
semantic_findings.description: The skill encourages manual Home Assistant automation triggers and service calls during verification. Depending on the target automation, these actions can affect locks, climate, lights, notifications, or other connected devices.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cited workflow directly invokes automation.trigger and common service-call commands. The impact depends on the user environment, but the physical-device side effect risk is clear.

content.value_statement: Home Assistant changes can be risky when deployments, reloads, and dashboards are handled manually. This skill gives Claude, Codex, and Claude Code structured workflows for validation, deployment, testing, and troubleshooting.
actual_capabilities: Explains SSH and hass-cli patterns for Home Assistant state checks, service calls, logs, reloads, and restarts.
Recommends git or scp deployment workflows based on whether changes are final or still being tested.
Guides automation verification with configuration checks, manual triggers, log review, and outcome confirmation.
Provides Lovelace dashboard guidance for storage files, dashboard registration, view types, card choices, and tablet layouts.
Includes Jinja2 template patterns and debugging guidance for common Home Assistant type and card errors.
Documents quick-reference commands for configuration validation, deployment, dashboard validation, and troubleshooting.
limitations: Requires an existing Home Assistant instance with SSH access, hass-cli, and valid user-provided credentials.
Can guide commands that change devices, dashboards, automations, or Home Assistant service state.
Does not replace backups, least-privilege credential practices, or review of generated configuration before deployment.
Cannot verify real device behavior unless the assistant has approved access to the user environment.

use_cases.title: Deploy Home Assistant configuration changes
use_cases.description: Plan validation, deployment, reload, restart, and verification steps for YAML, scripts, scenes, and template entities.

use_cases.title: Debug automation failures
use_cases.description: Use logs, manual triggers, state checks, and template fixes to isolate and resolve automation errors.

use_cases.title: Build tablet-friendly Lovelace dashboards
use_cases.description: Create dashboard layouts, choose card types, register storage dashboards, and iterate with quick preview workflows.

prompt_templates.title: Check my setup
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my Home Assistant project setup and tell me what SSH, hass-cli, git, and environment prerequisites are missing before I deploy changes.

prompt_templates.title: Deploy an automation safely
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me create and deploy a Home Assistant automation, then choose the safest reload or restart path and verification steps.

prompt_templates.title: Troubleshoot a dashboard issue
prompt_templates.prompt: Debug why my Lovelace dashboard is not appearing or has card errors, and guide me through validation, registration, deployment, and browser checks.

prompt_templates.title: Design a full workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Create an end-to-end Home Assistant change workflow that covers local edits, validation, rapid testing, git history, deployment, rollback, logs, and user confirmation gates.

output_examples.input: User asks to add a front door notification automation.
output_examples.output: The assistant proposes the automation behavior, identifies required entities, recommends a reload instead of a restart, and lists validation, trigger, log, and notification checks.

output_examples.input: User asks why a dashboard does not show in the sidebar.
output_examples.output: The assistant checks whether the dashboard file exists, whether it is registered, whether a restart is required, and whether the browser cache needs refresh.

output_examples.input: User reports a template comparison error.
output_examples.output: The assistant explains the likely type mismatch, recommends template casting, then outlines how to test the template and confirm logs are clean.

best_practices: Confirm target host, files, and expected device effects before running SSH, scp, hass-cli, reload, restart, or trigger commands.
Validate configuration and dashboard syntax before deployment, then review logs and user-visible outcomes after deployment.
Use scp for temporary iteration, git for stable changes, and backups before editing Home Assistant storage files.
anti_patterns: Do not store long-lived Home Assistant tokens in shared shell profiles, repositories, chat logs, or screenshots.
Do not restart Home Assistant when a targeted reload can safely apply the change.
Do not overwrite .storage dashboard files or trigger automations without user approval and a rollback plan.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps plan Home Assistant configuration edits, deployments, automation checks, log review, and Lovelace dashboard workflows.

faq.question: Does it require access to my Home Assistant server?
faq.answer: Yes. The documented workflows require user-approved SSH access, hass-cli access, and Home Assistant credentials.

faq.question: Can it create dashboards?
faq.answer: It provides patterns for Lovelace dashboards, storage files, dashboard registration, view selection, and tablet-friendly layouts.

faq.question: Can it change devices in my home?
faq.answer: It can guide service calls and automation triggers that may affect devices if the user approves those commands.

faq.question: Is this only for Claude Code?
faq.answer: The skill is written for Claude Code style workflows, and the marketplace metadata also lists Claude and Codex compatibility.

faq.question: What should I review before using it?
faq.answer: Review credentials, target host, command approvals, backups, generated configuration, and any automation that can affect physical devices.
